Does water boiled at a lower atmospheric pressure at a lower temperature purify as effectively as water boiled at 1 atmosphere at 100 Celsius?

No. Boiling water to kill unsafe micro-organisms and purifying water are two different things. Water purification is achieved through fractional distillation, in which all the components in water (any chemical contaminants, flora and fauna, etc.) have different boiling temperatures and pressures than H2O. The H2O is isolated and the other things are either discarded or further refined. Pharmaceutical grade distilled water is often run through fractional distillation multiple times so only H2O is present.

Boiling water is not sufficient to purify it, but it may still be safe to drink. All the dead flora and fauna bodies will still be in it, but hopefully they will be neutralized from causing disease. However, if the flora and fauna that would be killed at 100C @1atm are able to survive the boiling at other pressures, then they will still cause infection. If there were any chemical contaminants they will still likely be present unless they have a lower boiling point than water, such as alcohol. Activated carbon is often used to capture the free floating dead flora and fauna and some chemical contaminants.
So it is the 100C temperature that does the killing making safe to drink.
Depends on the amount of time - that's the other factor that needs to be included.

Yes, although this is a guide more than a law. There are extremophile critters that thrive in high temperature, acid, and radioactive environments that would melt the skin off humans' faces. So far none of the flora or fauna that cause infections in humans have exhibited extremeophile survival traits, such as multiple DNA copies per cell or robust cell walls. However, with the amount of antibiotics and water detergents we've been using for the last century, our guide may not hold true forever- life...a...a finds a way.

Clostridium botulinum has extremophile traits, without being an extremophile, it exhibits those traits when it is a spore, and it will kill you in a most unpleasant way..

Fortunately it isn't found in water. It is found in honey, but generally it doesn't harm adults (just gives them grotesque faces). But it will kill a baby. So don't feed your baby honey.

Exposing it to serious vacuum to drop the boiling temperature might be pretty effective actually. I'm thinking vacuum drying, not just boiling it but sucking all the water out of the system through the vacuum pump as micron measured vapor (this is not a fast process though).
